Compiler::Compiler API compatibility.summary: TypeScript 7.0 has no compiler API yet. Run its `tsc` alongside a TypeScript 6 compatibility package so API-dependent tools such as typescript-eslint can continue using the TypeScript 6 API.
Compiler::Compiler API compatibility.explanation: TypeScript 7.0 does not provide its own compiler API yet. Install TypeScript 7 for the `tsc` command and use the companion package that re-exports the TypeScript 6 API, exposing `tsc6` so API-dependent tooling can continue using TypeScript 6 without a naming conflict.
Compiler::Compiler API compatibility.syntax:
npm install --save-dev typescript@7 typescript-tsc6
npx tsc
npx tsc6

example.title: Run TypeScript 7 and TypeScript 6 side by side
example.code:
npm install --save-dev typescript@7 typescript-tsc6
npx tsc --version
npx tsc6 --version
example.explanation: Installs TypeScript 7 while preserving a separate TypeScript 6 compiler executable for tools that still require the older API.

useCases.title: Incremental tool migration
useCases.scenario: A project wants TypeScript 7’s compiler while its linting integration still consumes the older compiler API.

useCases.title: Side-by-side compiler execution
useCases.scenario: A repository needs both compiler generations available during the API transition.

useCases.title: Temporary API compatibility
useCases.scenario: A build uses TypeScript 7 but a utility has not yet adopted the future TypeScript 7.1 API.

interview.question: Why might a tool still use TypeScript 6 when the project uses TypeScript 7?
interview.answer: TypeScript 7.0 does not ship with an API. The supported transition is to run TypeScript 7’s `tsc` while compiler-dependent utilities continue using the re-exported TypeScript 6.0 API.
interview.followUp: What changes in TypeScript 7.1? The documentation expects a new and different API, so consumers should avoid assuming TypeScript 6 API compatibility will continue.

interview.question: How can both compiler versions be installed together?
interview.answer: The companion package exposes a `tsc6` executable and re-exports the TypeScript 6.0 API. This lets TypeScript 7 and TypeScript 6 operate side by side without executable-name collisions.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid accidentally invoking the old compiler? Call `tsc` for TypeScript 7 and explicitly invoke `tsc6` only for API-dependent tooling.

interview.question: Which kind of tooling is covered by this compatibility arrangement?
interview.answer: The documented example is `typescript-eslint`, which still needs programmatic compiler access. Such utilities can remain on the TypeScript 6 API while the project’s command-line compiler moves to TypeScript 7.
interview.followUp: What should an API consumer do for a future migration? Track the TypeScript 7.1 API and update against that new, different surface rather than relying indefinitely on the compatibility package.

keyPoints: A companion package makes the TypeScript 6.0 API available while TypeScript 7 is installed.
Use the normal `tsc` command for TypeScript 7 compilation.
API-dependent tools can remain on TypeScript 6 during the transition.
The documentation names typescript-eslint as an example of a utility that still needs compiler access.
The compatibility package supplies a distinct `tsc6` command for TypeScript 6.
gotchas: Do not assume compiler-API consumers can migrate directly to TypeScript 7.0; its API is not included.
Plan for another API migration when TypeScript 7.1 arrives rather than treating the TypeScript 6 compatibility layer as permanent.
Use the separate `tsc6` executable when both compiler generations are installed.

Compiler::Parallel builds.summary: TypeScript 7 parallelizes compilation and project-reference builds. Tune checker and builder worker counts with --checkers and --builders, or disable concurrency with --singleThreaded.
Compiler::Parallel builds.explanation: TypeScript 7 parallelizes parsing, checking, emitting, and project-reference builds. Use --checkers to set type-checker workers, --builders to control concurrent project builders under --build, or --singleThreaded to turn parallelism off.

parameters.name: --checkers
parameters.description: Number of type-checker workers.

parameters.name: --builders
parameters.description: Number of concurrent project-reference builders used with --build.

parameters.name: --singleThreaded
parameters.description: Disables parallelization.

example.title: Tune parallel build workers
example.code: tsgo --build --checkers 8 --builders 4
example.explanation: Runs a project-reference build with eight type-checker workers and four parallel project builders.

useCases.title: Increase checking throughput
useCases.scenario: A large repository has spare CPU capacity during CI builds.

useCases.title: Parallelize project builds
useCases.scenario: A project-reference monorepo needs multiple packages built concurrently.

useCases.title: Simplify debugging with one thread
useCases.scenario: A compiler failure is difficult to reproduce or inspect.

interview.question: How do you tune parallel TypeScript 7 builds?
interview.answer: TypeScript 7 parallelizes parsing, type-checking, and emitting, and it can build several project references concurrently. The --checkers flag controls type-checker workers, while --builders controls concurrent project-reference builders under --build.
interview.followUp: Why are separate controls useful? Type-checking and project-reference scheduling are different workloads, so independently sizing their worker pools lets a repository tune each bottleneck.

interview.question: What is the default checker-worker behavior?
interview.answer: The default type-checking worker count is four. Increase or decrease it with --checkers according to available CPU and memory, then measure the result on the target repository.
interview.followUp: What should you do when parallel output is difficult to diagnose? Re-run with --singleThreaded to remove parallel execution and simplify debugging.

interview.question: When should single-threaded mode be used?
interview.answer: Use --singleThreaded when debugging or when the environment has limited resources. It disables the compiler's parallelization rather than merely reducing worker counts.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve concurrency while reducing pressure? Prefer lowering --checkers and --builders first, because that retains parallel work while limiting simultaneous workers.

keyPoints: Parallelism covers the main compilation pipeline: parsing, type-checking, and output generation.
Large repositories benefit because independent file work can proceed concurrently without large coordination costs.
Set --checkers to tune the number of type-checker workers.
Set --builders to control how many project-reference builders run simultaneously.
Project-reference builds gain cross-project concurrency in addition to within-project parallel work.
Checker workers use isolated views, allowing type-checking to run concurrently without sharing one mutable checker state.
gotchas: Using --singleThreaded removes parallel execution, so reserve it for debugging or resource-constrained environments.
Changing --checkers is optional; the compiler already starts with four type-checking workers.
Treat these tuning flags as experimental and validate them in your build environment before standardizing them.

Compiler::tsc and project references.summary: Project references split a TypeScript repository into smaller, connected projects. The tsc --build mode follows those dependencies, skips up-to-date work, and builds stale projects in the required order.
Compiler::tsc and project references.explanation: Project references connect separate tsconfig.json projects through a references array. With composite projects and declaration output, tsc --build can discover dependencies, reuse up-to-date outputs, and rebuild projects in dependency order.

parameters.name: references[].path
parameters.description: A directory containing tsconfig.json or a path to a configuration file.

Compiler::tsc and project references.returns: Build mode updates out-of-date referenced projects and their dependencies in dependency order.

example.title: Referenced project configuration
example.explanation: Make the referenced project composite and emit declarations so the consuming project can use its build output.

useCases.title: Separate repository components
useCases.scenario: A monorepo contains libraries and applications with clear dependency boundaries.

useCases.title: Shorten incremental builds
useCases.scenario: Only some projects change between commits.

useCases.title: Enforce declaration-based boundaries
useCases.scenario: A consumer should type-check against a library’s public output.

interview.question: What does tsconfig.json references do?
interview.answer: The references property is an array of objects that identifies dependent tsconfig projects, usually with a path to a directory or config file. It describes the project graph so build mode can process dependencies before consumers.
interview.followUp: What does a path reference accept? It can point to a directory containing tsconfig.json or directly to a configuration file with any name.

interview.question: How does tsc --build use project references?
interview.answer: tsc --build, abbreviated tsc -b, finds referenced projects, checks which are up to date, and builds outdated projects in dependency order. It can also receive multiple configuration paths.
interview.followUp: Why can this be faster? Up-to-date projects are skipped, while only stale projects and the required dependency chain are rebuilt.

interview.question: Why is composite required?
interview.answer: The composite option is required on referenced projects because it lets TypeScript determine their outputs quickly. Composite projects also require every implementation file to be included or explicitly listed.
interview.followUp: What does a consumer load from a referenced project? It loads the referenced project's emitted declaration file, such as a .d.ts output.

keyPoints: Use project references to divide a large TypeScript program into separately buildable projects.
The arrangement can improve build performance, strengthen component boundaries, and provide clearer organization.
Declare project dependencies with the top-level references property in tsconfig.json.
Each reference path may identify a config-containing directory or the configuration file directly.
Build mode can build a referenced dependency automatically when its outputs are needed.
Build mode checks project freshness before deciding whether compilation is necessary.
When rebuilding, tsc --build follows dependency order so prerequisites are compiled first.
gotchas: Every referenced project must enable composite.
Composite projects must account for every implementation file through files or include.
A consumer type-checks against the referenced project's emitted declarations rather than its implementation source.

Compiler::TypeScript language service.summary: TypeScript’s language service powers TypeScript and JavaScript editor features such as diagnostics, completion, navigation, and quick fixes. In TypeScript 7, its native implementation aims to improve editor startup, responsiveness, memory use, and parallelism.
Compiler::TypeScript language service.explanation: The TypeScript language service powers editor features for TypeScript and JavaScript, including diagnostics, completion, navigation, refactoring support, and other interactive tooling. In TypeScript 7, the service is part of the native compiler and uses the Language Server Protocol so modern editors can communicate with it efficiently.
Compiler::TypeScript language service.returns: Editor-language features and diagnostics for TypeScript and JavaScript files.

example.title: Editor diagnostics
example.explanation: Open this file in a TypeScript 7-enabled editor to see a diagnostic and use editor navigation or completion on `user`.

useCases.title: Diagnostics and completions
useCases.scenario: Editing TypeScript or JavaScript in a supported editor

useCases.title: Definition and reference navigation
useCases.scenario: Tracing a symbol through a codebase

useCases.title: Quick fixes and refactoring
useCases.scenario: Repairing common editor-detected issues

interview.question: What is the TypeScript language service?
interview.answer: The language service is the component that supplies TypeScript and JavaScript editor functionality. It handles features such as completions, hover information, navigation, references, rename, formatting, and quick fixes.
interview.followUp: Why does TypeScript 7 change the implementation? The service is being ported to native code to improve execution speed, memory use, and parallelism.

interview.question: What benefits does the native language service provide?
interview.answer: TypeScript 7 places the language service on the native compiler foundation. The native implementation is intended to improve editor startup, project loading, and responsiveness for operations such as completion, quick info, definition lookup, and reference search.
interview.followUp: What editor integration protocol does the newer foundation use? It uses the Language Server Protocol, allowing support across modern editors and related tools.

interview.question: Which editor features are powered by the language service?
interview.answer: The service exposes interactive tooling rather than only command-line checking. Its documented capabilities include code completion, go-to-definition, find-all-references, rename, signature help, formatting, code lenses, document symbols, and quick fixes for missing imports.
interview.followUp: Which capability may differ during the preview? Find All References may appear as a flat list and cross-file references can be incomplete.

keyPoints: The language service is the editor-facing layer for TypeScript and JavaScript development.
Completion lists can include automatically suggested imports.
The service supports jumping from a symbol to its definition.
It can locate references to a symbol across the project.
Hovering over code can reveal contextual type and symbol information.
The service can suggest fixes when an import is missing.

Compiler::What TypeScript 7 is.summary: TypeScript 7 is the native Go-based port of the TypeScript compiler and tools. It preserves the familiar `tsc` workflow and type-checking model while adding native speed, shared-memory parallelism, and substantial build-performance improvements.
Compiler::What TypeScript 7 is.explanation: TypeScript 7 is a native implementation of the TypeScript compiler and tools, ported to Go while preserving the existing codebase's structure and behavior. It keeps the familiar command-line workflow and type-checking model, while using native execution, shared-memory parallelism, and optimizations to reduce build time and memory use.

example.title: Use the TypeScript 7 compiler
example.code:
npm install -D typescript@7
npx tsc --noEmit
example.explanation: Install TypeScript 7 as a project dependency, then run its familiar compiler command to type-check the project.

useCases.title: Accelerate compilation
useCases.scenario: Large repositories with slow full builds

useCases.title: Shorten continuous-integration checks
useCases.scenario: CI pipelines constrained by build duration

useCases.title: Retain the existing tsc workflow
useCases.scenario: Teams migrating from the JavaScript compiler without changing scripts

useCases.title: Run TypeScript 7 alongside TypeScript 6
useCases.scenario: Projects needing a staged major-version transition

interview.question: What is TypeScript 7?
interview.answer: TypeScript 7 is the native port of the TypeScript compiler and tools, built in Go. Its purpose is to improve raw execution speed, memory usage, and parallelism while retaining compatible compiler behavior.
interview.followUp: What migration strategy supports projects that cannot move immediately? Keep TypeScript 6 available and upgrade to TypeScript 7 when its compatibility requirements are satisfied.

interview.question: What performance improvements does TypeScript 7 provide?
interview.answer: The native implementation uses native execution speed, shared-memory multithreading, and additional optimizations. The documented result is typically an 8x to 12x speedup on full builds.
interview.followUp: Why can speedups vary? Workload, project structure, hardware, and the portion of the toolchain being measured affect the observed result.

interview.question: How does TypeScript 7 affect the existing `tsc` workflow?
interview.answer: TypeScript 7 can be installed from the `typescript` npm package like other releases, and it ships the familiar `tsc` binary. This lets existing command-line type-checking workflows continue using the usual command.
interview.followUp: How can TypeScript 6 remain available during migration? The compatibility package `@typescript/typescript6` provides a separate `tsc6` executable and re-exports the TypeScript 6 API.

keyPoints: TypeScript 7 is the current native major release of the TypeScript compiler and its supporting tools.
The native port is designed to make compilation substantially faster than the previous JavaScript-based implementation.
The compiler was reimplemented natively in Go rather than continuing as a bootstrapped JavaScript codebase.
Its main architectural gains come from native execution and shared-memory parallelism.
Full-build performance commonly improves by roughly an order of magnitude, although exact gains depend on the workload.
TypeScript 7 keeps the standard `tsc` executable, so common scripts and command-line checks can remain familiar.

Configuration::exactOptionalPropertyType.summary: Distinguishes an omitted optional property from one explicitly assigned undefined. When enabled, an optional property accepts only its written value type when present; add | undefined if explicit undefined should be allowed.
Configuration::exactOptionalPropertyType.explanation: The option changes optional-property checking so a question-mark property accepts its declared values when present, while omission remains valid. To permit an explicit undefined value, include | undefined in the property type; strictNullChecks must also be enabled.

example.title: Exact optional property assignment
example.explanation: Compile with strictNullChecks and exactOptionalPropertyTypes enabled. The property may be omitted, but an explicit undefined assignment is rejected.

useCases.title: Represent inherited defaults
useCases.scenario: Configuration objects where omission means inherit a default.

useCases.title: Preserve presence semantics
useCases.scenario: APIs that need to distinguish an absent field from a field intentionally set to undefined.

useCases.title: Tighten object contracts
useCases.scenario: Migration from permissive optional-property behavior to declarations that match runtime checks.

interview.question: What does exactOptionalPropertyTypes change?
interview.answer: It makes TypeScript interpret optional property types exactly as written instead of implicitly adding undefined. Thus colorThemeOverride?: "dark" | "light" permits omission and those two strings, but not an explicit undefined assignment.
interview.followUp: How would you permit explicit undefined? Add | undefined to the declared property type.

interview.question: Is it included in strict?
interview.answer: No. The flag is separate from the strict family and must be enabled explicitly. It also requires strictNullChecks.
interview.followUp: What happens if strictNullChecks is disabled? The documented prerequisite is not satisfied, so enable strictNullChecks before relying on this option.

interview.question: Why distinguish omission from explicit undefined?
interview.answer: An omitted property and a present property whose value is undefined are different object states. The option enforces that distinction for optional properties, matching the declared type when the property exists.
interview.followUp: Why does that distinction matter? Runtime checks for property existence can distinguish those states even though both may produce undefined-like behavior in some access patterns.

keyPoints: The option applies stricter checking to optional properties declared with ?.
An omitted option can deliberately represent a separate state, such as inheriting a system default.
A ? modifier does not automatically mean the declared value may be explicitly undefined when this option is enabled.
Assignments are checked against the written optional-property type rather than a widened version.
Assigning undefined to an optional property whose declared values exclude it produces a type error.
gotchas: It is not enabled by the strict family, so configure it explicitly.
The option depends on strictNullChecks being enabled.
Explicit undefined can undermine runtime presence checks, so use omission when absence is intended.

Configuration::Modules and resolution.summary: TypeScript’s moduleResolution setting maps module specifiers to files using rules that should match Node.js or a bundler. Modern projects generally choose nodenext/node16 for Node.js or bundler for bundler-controlled builds.
Configuration::Modules and resolution.explanation: TypeScript resolves each module specifier according to the host you target. Use Node-oriented resolution for modern Node.js, where imports and require can follow different algorithms, or bundler resolution when a bundler handles the final module graph; the selected mode also determines package exports/imports behavior and whether relative extensions are required.

parameters.name: moduleResolution
parameters.description: Resolution strategy used for module specifiers; modern choices include node16, nodenext, and bundler.

example.title: Node-style ESM import
example.explanation: With Node-style ESM, the import uses the emitted JavaScript extension; TypeScript resolves the corresponding source or declaration file.

useCases.title: Model Node.js module loading
useCases.scenario: A package runs directly under modern Node.js and may emit both import and require.

useCases.title: Model bundler resolution
useCases.scenario: A frontend or library build relies on a bundler to resolve the complete dependency graph.

useCases.title: Check published declaration compatibility
useCases.scenario: A package exposes declarations whose preserved imports must work for downstream consumers.

interview.question: Which resolver should a modern Node.js project use?
interview.answer: Set moduleResolution to nodenext or node16 for modern Node.js projects, and pair it with the corresponding module setting. These modes account for whether emitted JavaScript uses import or require, because Node resolves those forms differently.
interview.followUp: Why not use bundler for a Node application? Bundler mode permits extensionless relative imports, which may not resolve when Node executes the emitted files directly.

interview.question: When is moduleResolution bundler appropriate?
interview.answer: Use bundler when a bundler owns module resolution and the project can rely on its behavior. This mode supports package.json imports and exports while allowing extensionless relative imports.
interview.followUp: What if declarations are consumed externally? Use Node-oriented resolution when declarations preserve imports that must work under end users’ TypeScript and runtime settings.

interview.question: How does TypeScript resolve types without changing runtime behavior?
interview.answer: TypeScript first seeks a TypeScript implementation or declaration corresponding to a JavaScript lookup, while keeping the resolved path compatible with the runtime or bundler’s implementation. This lets checking use types without changing the host’s intended module path.
interview.followUp: What package metadata matters? The resolver uses package.json imports and exports in the supported Node and bundler modes, so package boundaries and conditions affect the selected file.

keyPoints: The moduleResolution option selects the algorithm used to map import, export, and require specifiers to files.
Choose the resolver according to the actual host that will load the emitted code, not merely according to source syntax.
During resolution, TypeScript looks for source or declaration counterparts before settling on the JavaScript implementation path.
gotchas: A project that both bundles some imports and externalizes others cannot model both resolver behaviors in one compilation.

Configuration::noUncheckedIndexedAccess.summary: Makes indexed and undeclared property lookups include undefined, reflecting that the requested key may be absent at runtime. Code must narrow the result or explicitly assert that it exists.
Configuration::noUncheckedIndexedAccess.explanation: Enable this compiler option when index signatures or indexed collections represent keys that may be absent at runtime. TypeScript then adds undefined to undeclared property and indexed-access results, requiring an existence check or an explicitly justified non-null assertion before the value is used.

parameters.name: noUncheckedIndexedAccess
parameters.description: Boolean compiler option; the documented compiler-options reference lists its default as false.

Configuration::noUncheckedIndexedAccess.returns: Not applicable; this is a compiler option that changes the types produced for property and indexed accesses.

example.title: Safely reading an undeclared key
example.explanation: The declared NAME property remains string, while a lookup for an undeclared key becomes string | undefined and therefore must be checked before use.

useCases.title: Model optional keys in index-signature objects
useCases.scenario: Reading configuration or environment dictionaries

useCases.title: Catch potentially missing elements
useCases.scenario: Accessing arrays or tuples by a computed numeric index

useCases.title: Expose unsafe lookups during strictness adoption
useCases.scenario: Migrating code that assumes every dynamic key exists

interview.question: What does noUncheckedIndexedAccess change?
interview.answer: It changes the type of an undeclared lookup covered by an index signature by adding undefined. A declared property such as env.NAME keeps its declared type, while env.NODE_ENV becomes string | undefined.
interview.followUp: What must code do before calling a method on that result? Narrow it with an existence check, or use a non-null assertion when the runtime invariant is genuinely guaranteed.

interview.question: Why is this option useful with index signatures?
interview.answer: It makes arbitrary property and indexed accesses potentially undefined because the key may not exist at runtime. This applies to both dot-style property access and bracket-style indexed access in the documented examples.
interview.followUp: Does bracket notation avoid the check? No; the option specifically checks indexed access, and the documentation also shows property access being affected.

interview.question: Does the option affect arrays?
interview.answer: The option also makes array indexing stricter. Even a loop that checks an index against an array's length can still produce a possibly undefined element type under this mode.
interview.followUp: How should a migration handle such errors? Narrow the element before use, or redesign the access so the type system can establish that an element is present.

keyPoints: Index signatures describe a value type for keys that are not individually declared.
The option augments undeclared fields with undefined instead of assuming every possible key exists.
Both dot access and bracket access can become possibly undefined when the option is enabled.
A lookup's resulting union preserves the index-signature value types and adds undefined.
Array indexing participates in the stricter checking rather than remaining an unchecked special case.
gotchas: Array element reads are checked too, including reads performed inside a bounds-checked loop.
After a lookup becomes possibly undefined, either prove the property exists or use the postfix ! operator with care.

Configuration::Strict compiler checks.summary: Enable TypeScript's strict compiler option to turn on the full strict-mode family of checks. Keep it enabled for stronger compile-time guarantees, selectively relaxing individual checks only when necessary.
Configuration::Strict compiler checks.explanation: Set the compiler's strict master option to enable TypeScript's strongest family of type checks. Individual strict checks can still be disabled when migration constraints require it, while future compiler versions may add stricter checks under the master option.

parameters.name: strict
parameters.description: Master compiler setting that enables the strict mode family; individual family options may override it.

example.title: Strict checking catches nullable misuse
example.explanation: With strict checking enabled, the call must handle the possibility that value is undefined.

useCases.title: Start with stronger type guarantees
useCases.scenario: New projects

useCases.title: Adopt strict checks incrementally by disabling only specific blockers
useCases.scenario: Migration

useCases.title: Prevent newly introduced invalid states from compiling
useCases.scenario: CI builds

interview.question: What does TypeScript's strict compiler option do?
interview.answer: The strict option enables the complete strict-mode family of type-checking options. It is equivalent to enabling those options individually, and it produces stronger guarantees of program correctness.
interview.followUp: Can one strict check be relaxed during migration? Yes. Keep strict enabled and set the specific strict-family option to false.

interview.question: How does strictNullChecks make invalid states visible?
interview.answer: With strictNullChecks enabled, null and undefined have distinct types. Passing a possibly undefined value where a concrete value is required therefore produces a type error.
interview.followUp: What is the migration-friendly alternative to disabling strict entirely? Preserve strict and selectively disable only the blocking strict-family check.

interview.question: How would you enable strict checking for a project?
interview.answer: strict is a compiler option, so it can be enabled in tsconfig.json under compilerOptions or supplied as a command-line option. The configuration applies the strict checks to the project compilation.
interview.followUp: What should be checked after changing it? Run the project compiler and address the newly reported errors, including any surfaced by a TypeScript upgrade.

keyPoints: strict activates a broad set of checks intended to provide stronger compile-time correctness guarantees.
The master flag represents the strict-mode family rather than a single isolated diagnostic.
A project can retain the master setting while opting out of selected checks for compatibility or staged migration.
Strict null checking separates nullish values from ordinary concrete types.
Code must account for null and undefined before using a value as definitely present.
gotchas: Upgrading TypeScript can reveal new errors when strict is enabled; treat compiler upgrades as potentially requiring fixes.
strict is not all-or-nothing: individual checks can be disabled, which can reduce the guarantees provided by the overall configuration.

Configuration::tsconfig migration.summary: TypeScript 7 removes deprecated compiler behaviors and options. Make target, module resolution, and directory layout explicit, and replace settings such as ES5, baseUrl, and node10 resolution.
Configuration::tsconfig migration.explanation: TypeScript 7 removes several older compiler behaviors and options, so migration means making the intended target and directory layout explicit and replacing obsolete module-resolution choices. Review deprecated settings, update configurations such as baseUrl and node10 resolution, and ensure rootDir is explicit when using outDir.

example.title: TypeScript 7-compatible tsconfig
example.explanation: This configuration makes the emitted JavaScript target explicit and replaces removed TypeScript 7-era assumptions about module resolution and root/output directories.

useCases.title: Stabilize emitted JavaScript
useCases.scenario: A project currently targets ES5 or relies on TypeScript’s changing default target.

useCases.title: Replace removed resolution settings
useCases.scenario: A project uses node10/node module resolution or baseUrl.

useCases.title: Preserve output directory structure
useCases.scenario: A project emits files with outDir and has nested source directories.

interview.question: Why should a project explicitly set target during a TypeScript 7 migration?
interview.answer: TypeScript 7 removes ES5 as a target, making ES2015 the lowest supported target. A migration should therefore select an explicit target that matches the runtimes the project supports.
interview.followUp: What happens if target is omitted? TypeScript 7 defaults target to the latest stable ECMAScript target, so omitting it can change emitted output during upgrades.

interview.question: Which module-resolution migration is required?
interview.answer: The legacy node10 module-resolution mode is removed. Projects should choose bundler or nodenext based on whether resolution follows a bundler or Node’s modern package rules.
interview.followUp: Why is node10 not a safe compatibility setting? It is one of the deprecated modes removed in TypeScript 7, so retaining it prevents a clean migration.

interview.question: How should rootDir and outDir be reviewed?
interview.answer: TypeScript 7 changes rootDir behavior: it defaults to the current directory, and outDir requires either an explicit rootDir or top-level source files beside tsconfig.json. Set rootDir deliberately when preserving an output layout.
interview.followUp: What related option may also require migration? baseUrl is removed, so path resolution should not rely on that setting.

keyPoints: Audit deprecated compiler flags and behaviors before upgrading, because TypeScript 7 removes the items deprecated in TypeScript 6.
Treat strict checking as an upcoming default and resolve newly exposed type errors rather than depending on strict being disabled.
Set target explicitly to prevent the generated JavaScript target from changing with a future TypeScript release.
Migration can require both source-code changes and tsconfig.json changes when deprecated behavior is part of the project.
gotchas: A configuration targeting ES5 will no longer be accepted; choose ES2015 or a newer target.
Do not depend on baseUrl for module lookup; migrate those imports and configuration patterns.
Replace the legacy node10/node module-resolution mode with bundler or nodenext as appropriate.
When outDir is used, define rootDir explicitly unless all source files are top-level beside tsconfig.json.

JavaScript interop::Declaration files.summary: Declaration files give JavaScript packages a publishable type surface for TypeScript consumers. Bundle generated or handwritten declarations with the package, or publish them separately through DefinitelyTyped under the @types scope.
JavaScript interop::Declaration files.explanation: Declaration files describe the types and values provided by an existing JavaScript package without implementing them. A package can ship its own .d.ts file, referenced through package.json, or its declarations can be published separately under the @types scope for consumers to discover.

example.title: Bundle declarations with a package
example.explanation: The package bundles a declaration file and points to it with the package.json types property, allowing a TypeScript consumer to check the imported API.

useCases.title: Bundle package types
useCases.scenario: A JavaScript or TypeScript library publishes its implementation and generated declarations together.

useCases.title: Publish via @types
useCases.scenario: A popular untyped npm library needs community-maintained declarations without changing its implementation package.

useCases.title: Advertise the declaration entry point
useCases.scenario: A package exposes a JavaScript entry point and needs TypeScript to locate its public API types.

interview.question: How do declaration files support JavaScript package consumers?
interview.answer: A declaration file supplies type information for an existing implementation, but does not contain that implementation. For a package with a main JavaScript file, publish the declaration alongside the package and set package.json's types property to its path.
interview.followUp: How can types be distributed when the package does not bundle them? Publish a separate declaration package through DefinitelyTyped, which is released under the @types scope.

interview.question: What are the main ways to publish declaration files?
interview.answer: The two documented publication routes are bundling declarations with the npm package or publishing them through the @types organization. If TypeScript generates the declarations from source, the generated files should be published with that source package.
interview.followUp: What is the recommended route for declarations maintained outside the package? Submit them to DefinitelyTyped so the types-publisher can publish an @types package.

interview.question: How does a package tell TypeScript where its bundled declarations are?
interview.answer: A bundled declaration file is selected by the types property in package.json. It should point to the declaration file corresponding to the package's main JavaScript entry point, so TypeScript can use the package's public types.
interview.followUp: What should be checked for declaration dependencies? Ensure dependent declaration packages are listed appropriately in the package.json dependencies section.

keyPoints: Publish declarations either inside the npm package or separately through the @types organization.
Generated declarations belong in the same published package as the source that produces them.
The declaration compiler option can generate types from both TypeScript and JavaScript projects.
When declarations are not generated and bundled, submit them to DefinitelyTyped for publication under @types.
Use package.json's types field to identify the bundled declaration entry file.
The @types publication flow automatically releases packages sourced from DefinitelyTyped.
gotchas: A package with a main JavaScript entry point must also identify its declaration entry point.
Declaration packages required at runtime or for the published package must be classified correctly in package.json dependencies.

JavaScript interop::Decorators and class.summary: Standard decorators let reusable code customize TypeScript classes and members without abandoning explicit public types. They support methods, fields, accessors, auto-accessors, and classes, including replacement or registration patterns.
JavaScript interop::Decorators and class.explanation: A standard decorator is an `@`-prefixed expression placed on a class or member. TypeScript supplies the decorated value and a context object, allowing reusable code to observe or replace methods, fields, accessors, or classes while keeping the class's public type contract explicit.
JavaScript interop::Decorators and class.returns: A decorator may return a replacement class or member definition; returning nothing leaves the original definition in place.

example.title: Wrapping a class method
example.explanation: The decorator wraps a class method, logs its name when called, and preserves the method's result.

useCases.title: Logging and tracing
useCases.scenario: Instrumenting methods

useCases.title: Automatic registration
useCases.scenario: Adding classes to a registry

useCases.title: Subclassing and customization
useCases.scenario: Replacing or extending class behavior

interview.question: What problem do decorators solve?
interview.answer: A decorator is an ECMAScript feature for customizing classes and their members. It is written with `@` and can replace or augment the decorated declaration through the value and context it receives.
interview.followUp: What additional class members can standard decorators target? They can target fields, getters, setters, auto-accessors, and the class itself.

interview.question: How can a decorator modify a method?
interview.answer: A method decorator receives the method value and a context describing the declaration. It can return a replacement function, which is useful for logging, validation, registration, or other reusable behavior.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve the method's public API? Type the replacement with the same parameter and return types, and avoid changing the class's externally visible contract.

interview.question: How do standard and legacy decorators differ?
interview.answer: Standard decorators are distinct from the older experimental TypeScript implementation. The experimental form requires `experimentalDecorators`, while the standard form follows the newer ECMAScript decorator design.
interview.followUp: Why should a migration check compiler settings and decorator signatures? Legacy and standard decorators differ in placement, runtime arguments, and supported behavior, so existing implementations may not be source- or behavior-compatible.

keyPoints: Decorators add reusable customization around class declarations and members.
Standard decorators support fields, getters, setters, and auto-accessors in addition to methods.
Decorating the class itself enables patterns such as registration and controlled subclassing.
Place a class decorator immediately before the class it decorates.
A class decorator operates on the constructor and may observe, modify, or replace the class definition.
Decorator syntax uses an `@` expression whose result is callable at runtime.
gotchas: Class decorators cannot annotate declaration files or ambient declarations such as `declare class`.
Decorators are not limited to methods; standard decorators also apply to fields, accessors, and classes.

JavaScript interop::JSDoc checking.summary: TypeScript can statically check .js files while they remain JavaScript. Enable checking per file with // @ts-check or across a project with checkJs, and add JSDoc when inference is insufficient.
JavaScript interop::JSDoc checking.explanation: TypeScript can check JavaScript files without requiring a conversion to .ts. Enable checking with // @ts-check in an individual .js file or with checkJs in compiler configuration, then use JSDoc annotations such as @type, @param, and @returns where inference is insufficient; use @ts-nocheck or @ts-ignore only when an intentional exception is needed.

example.title: Check a JavaScript file with JSDoc
example.explanation: Save this as a .js file and run the TypeScript compiler with JavaScript checking enabled, or open it in an editor with TypeScript support.

useCases.title: Incremental adoption
useCases.scenario: A JavaScript codebase needs diagnostics and editor assistance before any migration to .ts.

useCases.title: Document inferred gaps
useCases.scenario: A function's intended parameter or return type is not obvious from its implementation.

useCases.title: Selective file checking
useCases.scenario: Only selected legacy JavaScript files should receive static checking.

interview.question: How do you turn on type checking for JavaScript without renaming files?
interview.answer: Add // @ts-check at the top of a .js file to enable checking for that file. For a project-wide setting, use the checkJs compiler option; JSDoc supplies type information where inference cannot.
interview.followUp: How can checking be enabled selectively? Use // @ts-check for selected JavaScript files, while // @ts-nocheck disables checking for a file and // @ts-ignore suppresses a diagnostic on the following line.

interview.question: How does JSDoc add type information to JavaScript?
interview.answer: Place JSDoc before a declaration to describe its type, or annotate function parameters and results with tags such as @param and @returns. TypeScript uses those annotations during JavaScript checking and editor analysis.
interview.followUp: How can a type be reused across declarations? Define it with @typedef, then reference that named type from other JSDoc annotations.

interview.question: Name two checking differences between .js and .ts files.
interview.answer: JavaScript files have behavior that differs from TypeScript files: object literals are open-ended, and CommonJS assignments through exports or module.exports are understood as exports. Class property types are inferred from assignments in the class body.
interview.followUp: What happens when a class property is only read? Add a declaration in the constructor and annotate it with JSDoc so its type is explicit.

keyPoints: Put // @ts-check on the first line of a JavaScript file to request TypeScript diagnostics for that file.
Use a jsconfig.json when checking should cover many JavaScript files instead of adding a directive to each file.
Type inference handles many JavaScript cases; add JSDoc when the intended type cannot be inferred.
A JSDoc annotation immediately before a declaration supplies the declaration's type to TypeScript.
Use // @ts-nocheck to exclude an individual JavaScript file from TypeScript checking.
Suppress a known diagnostic for one line with // @ts-ignore or document an expected diagnostic with // @ts-expect-error.
gotchas: Initializing a variable, parameter, or property with null or undefined gives it type any, even when strict null checks is enabled.
JavaScript object literals remain open-ended, so properties can be added or read even when they were absent from the initial literal.
A property assigned in a constructor is treated as present, while one assigned only in methods, getters, or setters is considered optional.

JavaScript interop::Module augmentation.summary: Module augmentation lets you locally extend an existing module’s declarations, such as adding an application-specific method to a third-party class. Pair the type declaration with a runtime patch when the new member must actually execute.
JavaScript interop::Module augmentation.explanation: A module augmentation reopens an existing module with declare module and merges compatible declarations into the original as though they were declared together. It changes TypeScript’s view of the API, so a corresponding runtime patch is still needed when adding behavior; the consumer must load that patch module.

example.title: Add a map method to an existing class
example.explanation: The augmentation adds the method to the type, while the prototype assignment supplies its runtime implementation. Importing the patch module makes both available to the consumer.

useCases.title: Type a prototype extension
useCases.scenario: A dependency exposes a class whose runtime prototype is extended by application code.

useCases.title: Extend a package API
useCases.scenario: An application adds methods to a named export from a third-party package.

useCases.title: Patch global scope
useCases.scenario: A module needs additional global declarations while remaining a module.

interview.question: How do you write a module augmentation?
interview.answer: Use declare module with the target module’s specifier, then declare the additional member inside it. TypeScript merges that declaration with the original module’s declarations.
interview.followUp: What must happen if the addition changes runtime behavior? The augmentation only informs the compiler, so code must also patch the existing object or prototype and ensure that patch module is imported.

interview.question: What limitations apply to module augmentation?
interview.answer: An augmentation can patch existing declarations, but it cannot add new top-level declarations. It also cannot augment default exports; only named exports can be addressed by exported name.
interview.followUp: How are global augmentations constrained? They have the same behavior and limits as module augmentations, so they can patch existing global declarations but not add new top-level items.

interview.question: How does TypeScript locate and merge an augmentation?
interview.answer: The module specifier is resolved using the same rules as import and export specifiers. Declarations from the augmentation are merged as if they appeared in the original module’s file.
interview.followUp: Why can a consumer still fail at runtime after successful type-checking? Declaration merging affects types only; the implementation must be installed separately, commonly by importing the patch module.

keyPoints: Use module augmentation when a runtime extension needs a matching compile-time declaration.
The added declarations become part of the original module’s merged type view.
Target modules using the same resolution rules as ordinary import and export specifiers.
TypeScript’s declaration patch and JavaScript’s runtime patch are separate steps.
gotchas: An augmentation cannot introduce a new top-level export; it can only modify declarations already present in the target module.
Only named exports can be augmented; a default export cannot be targeted.
The string in declare module must resolve like an import or export specifier.

Migration::Migration from TypeScript 6.summary: Prepare on TypeScript 6 by enabling stable type ordering and fixing every deprecation, then install TypeScript 7 and verify the build. Keep API-dependent tools on @typescript/typescript6 until they support TypeScript 7’s compiler API.
Migration::Migration from TypeScript 6.explanation: First make the TypeScript 6 project clean with stable type ordering and without ignored deprecations. Then install TypeScript 7, run the compiler, and keep API-dependent tools on the TypeScript 6 compatibility package until they support the new API.

parameters.name: typescript@latest
parameters.description: TypeScript compiler package version selected for the project.

parameters.name: --noEmit
parameters.description: Suppress compiler output while still checking the project.

Migration::Migration from TypeScript 6.returns: A TypeScript 7 compiler installation and a successful no-emit type-check, with legacy API consumers isolated on the TypeScript 6 compatibility package.

example.title: Upgrade and verify
example.code:
npm install -D typescript@latest
npx tsc --noEmit
example.explanation: Install TypeScript 7 and run a no-output type check after removing deprecated options and updating dependent tooling.

useCases.title: Baseline the compiler migration
useCases.scenario: A project is moving from TypeScript 6 to 7 and wants predictable diagnostics.

useCases.title: Run API-dependent tooling during transition
useCases.scenario: A linter, transformer, or build tool still depends on the TypeScript 6 API.

useCases.title: Replace deprecated compiler settings
useCases.scenario: A configuration currently suppresses TypeScript 6 deprecation diagnostics.

interview.question: What is the recommended migration sequence?
interview.answer: Start by enabling stableTypeOrdering in TypeScript 6 and remove ignoreDeprecations. Fix every deprecation, then upgrade the compiler and verify that the project still type-checks.
interview.followUp: How can a tool that still needs the old compiler API coexist with TypeScript 7? Install @typescript/typescript6 and invoke its tsc6 entry point for that tool.

interview.question: How compatible is TypeScript 7 with TypeScript 6?
interview.answer: TypeScript 7 adopts TypeScript 6’s new defaults and turns TypeScript 6 deprecations into hard errors. Code that compiles under TypeScript 6 with stable type ordering enabled and no ignored deprecations should generally compile the same way.
interview.followUp: What should be checked if compilation changes anyway? Inspect deprecated flags, omitted stableTypeOrdering, module-resolution choices, and compiler-API dependencies.

interview.question: How should API-dependent tools be handled?
interview.answer: The @typescript/typescript6 package supplies a tsc6 executable and re-exports the TypeScript 6 API. This allows the TypeScript 7 compiler to be installed as tsc while API-dependent tooling temporarily continues using TypeScript 6.
interview.followUp: Why is this transitional arrangement needed? TypeScript 7.1 is expected to introduce a different API, so tools should migrate deliberately rather than assume API compatibility.

keyPoints: Install the compatibility package when a dependent tool still imports or calls the TypeScript 6 compiler API.
Use a clean TypeScript 6 build as the migration baseline before changing the compiler version.
Enable stableTypeOrdering during the TypeScript 6 verification pass to reduce type-ordering differences after upgrading.
Remove ignoreDeprecations and resolve the warnings rather than carrying suppressed deprecated behavior into TypeScript 7.
Expect TypeScript 7 to use the defaults introduced by TypeScript 6, so review configurations that relied on older defaults.
Use tsc6 for legacy compiler-API tooling while the regular tsc command belongs to TypeScript 7.
gotchas: Do not treat ignoreDeprecations as a long-term solution: TypeScript 7 removes support for options deprecated in TypeScript 6.
Compatibility covers type-checking and command-line behavior, but does not guarantee that tools using the compiler API can switch immediately.
Compiler-API consumers may need to remain on the TypeScript 6 API until their dependencies add TypeScript 7 support.

Type manipulation::Conditional and mappe.summary: Conditional types choose between types using an assignability test, while mapped types iterate over property keys to construct transformed object types. Together they support reusable, property-aware type transformations.
Type manipulation::Conditional and mappe.explanation: A conditional type selects one of two types by testing assignability with `extends`. A mapped type iterates over keys, optionally changes modifiers or remaps keys with `as`, and computes each property's value; combining both enables property-by-property transformations and filtering with `never`.
Type manipulation::Conditional and mappe.syntax:
T extends U ? X : Y

[Property in keyof Type]: Type[Property]

[Property in keyof Type as NewKey]: Type[Property]

parameters.name: T
parameters.description: The type being tested, iterated, or transformed.

parameters.name: U
parameters.description: The type relationship target in a conditional expression, or the source type whose keys are mapped.

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: The result when the conditional test succeeds.

parameters.name: Y
parameters.description: The result when the conditional test fails.

parameters.name: K
parameters.description: A property-key union used by a mapped type, often `keyof T`.

Type manipulation::Conditional and mappe.returns: A new type selected by a conditional branch, generated by mapping source keys, or both.

example.title: Remap and conditionally transform properties
example.explanation: The mapped type iterates over every key, remaps its name, and changes its value to string. The conditional mapped type chooses a result based on whether each property type extends boolean.

useCases.title: Adjust property modifiers
useCases.scenario: Create variants such as readonly, optional, nullable, or mutable views of an existing object type.

useCases.title: Remap or filter keys
useCases.scenario: Rename generated properties or exclude selected keys while deriving a new object type.

useCases.title: Conditionally transform fields
useCases.scenario: Choose a different property value type according to the original property's shape.

useCases.title: Keep related types synchronized
useCases.scenario: Derive reusable API, form, configuration, or validation types from a central model.

interview.question: What is a conditional type and what does its syntax mean?
interview.answer: The syntax is `T extends U ? X : Y`. If `T` is assignable to `U`, the result is `X`; otherwise it is `Y`. The compiler can defer the choice when type variables do not provide enough information.
interview.followUp: How does a conditional type distribute over a union? A naked checked type parameter causes the conditional to run independently for each union member, producing a union of the results.

interview.question: How does a mapped type transform an object type?
interview.answer: A mapped type iterates over a union of property keys, commonly `keyof T`, and creates a property for each key. The value expression can use the original property type, such as `T[K]`, to transform it.
interview.followUp: How can a mapped type omit properties? Use key remapping with `as` and produce `never` for keys that should be excluded.

interview.question: How do mapped types handle modifiers and key remapping?
interview.answer: Mapped types can alter property modifiers with `readonly` and `?`. Prefixing a modifier with `+` adds it, while prefixing with `-` removes it.
interview.followUp: How can mapped and conditional types work together? Use a conditional value expression to choose each property's result, or use a conditional `as` clause to filter keys.

keyPoints: Conditional types choose between two result types by testing whether one type is assignable to another.
Mapped types iterate through a key union, commonly obtained with `keyof`, to construct a new object type.
Mapped modifiers control whether generated properties are readonly and whether they are optional.
An `as` clause changes generated property names during mapping.
Combining conditional and mapped types supports transformations whose result depends on each property's type.
gotchas: A conditional type applied to a naked type parameter distributes over a union, evaluating each member separately; wrap the parameter in a tuple when you need one whole-union check.
Key remapping can remove properties by producing `never` for their remapped key.
When generic information is insufficient to decide the assignability test, evaluation is deferred rather than immediately selecting a branch.
Mapped modifiers affect readonly and optional properties; use `+` or `-` prefixes when the transformation must explicitly add or remove one.

Type manipulation::Indexed access types.summary: Indexed access types derive a property or array element type from an existing type with Type[Key]. Keys may be literals, unions, keyof expressions, or number for array elements.
Type manipulation::Indexed access types.explanation: Indexed access types use Type[Key] to retrieve a property type from another type. The key can be a literal, a union, keyof Type, or number for array elements; combining typeof with number derives the element type of an array value.

parameters.name: Type
parameters.description: The type being inspected; it may be an object, array, tuple, or another indexable type.

parameters.name: Key
parameters.description: A type representing a permitted property key or array index, such as a string literal, union, keyof Type, or number.

Type manipulation::Indexed access types.returns: The property, element, or indexed value type selected by Key from Type.

example.title: Derive element and property types
example.explanation: The array element type is obtained with typeof people[number], then its individual property types are selected with indexed access.

useCases.title: Reuse a model's property type
useCases.scenario: A shared model has properties consumed in several APIs, and those APIs should stay synchronized when the model changes.

useCases.title: Type-safe property lookup
useCases.scenario: A function receives a property name and must return the corresponding value type safely.

useCases.title: Derive types from array values
useCases.scenario: An array literal defines the source data, and a separate alias needs its element or nested property type.

related: TypeScript Handbook: Creating Types from Types

interview.question: What is an indexed access type?
interview.answer: The syntax is Type[Key]. For example, Person["age"] resolves to number because it looks up the age property's type on Person.
interview.followUp: What does Person["age" | "name"] produce? It produces the union of the selected property types, number | string.

interview.question: Which kinds of keys can indexed access types use?
interview.answer: The key position is itself a type, so it can be a union or keyof Person. A union key looks up each member and combines the resulting property types into a union.
interview.followUp: What does Person[keyof Person] represent? It is the union of all property value types in Person.

interview.question: How do indexed access types derive array element types?
interview.answer: For an array type, indexing with number retrieves its element type. With an array value, typeof MyArray[number] first captures the array's element type, which can then be indexed again for a property.
interview.followUp: How would you obtain the age type from an inferred array literal? Use typeof MyArray[number]["age"].

keyPoints: Use Type["property"] to derive a property's type without duplicating the property's declaration.
The key expression can be a literal union, keyof Type, or another type that resolves to permitted keys.
ArrayType[number] extracts the common element type from an array type.
typeof ArrayValue[number] derives an element type directly from an existing array value.
Indexed access can be chained: first select an array element, then select one of that element's properties.
gotchas: The index must be a type, not a value variable. Replace a const key with a type alias or another type expression.
The selected property must exist on the indexed type; misspelled or unsupported keys produce a compiler error.

Type manipulation::Infer in conditional.summary: Use `infer` inside a conditional type’s `extends` pattern to capture a matching part of a type and reuse it in the true branch. This enables reusable extraction utilities for elements, return types, parameters, and similar structures.
Type manipulation::Infer in conditional.explanation: Place `infer` inside the `extends` pattern of a conditional type to introduce a type variable that TypeScript derives from the compared type. That variable is available in the true branch, allowing reusable transformations to extract parts such as array elements, function return types, or parameter tuples.
Type manipulation::Infer in conditional.syntax: type Result<T> = T extends Pattern<infer U> ? TrueBranch<U> : FalseBranch<T>
Type manipulation::Infer in conditional.returns: The inferred type from the matched pattern in the true branch; otherwise, the conditional type's false-branch result.

example.title: Extract an array element type
example.explanation: The conditional type extracts an array element type when the input is an array; otherwise, it preserves the original type.

useCases.title: Extract array elements
useCases.scenario: A generic type may be an array or a scalar, and the transformation should expose its element type only for arrays.

useCases.title: Extract function return types
useCases.scenario: A utility needs the output type of a function without requiring callers to specify it separately.

useCases.title: Extract parameter tuples
useCases.scenario: A higher-order utility needs to preserve or inspect a function's argument tuple.

useCases.title: Inspect tuple structure
useCases.scenario: A tuple transformation needs to inspect a particular position, such as its first element.

interview.question: What does `infer` do in a conditional type?
interview.answer: `infer` declares a type variable within the `extends` pattern of a conditional type. If the checked type matches that pattern, the inferred variable can be used in the true branch.
interview.followUp: How would you extract a function’s return type? Define `T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never`; `R` is the inferred return type.

interview.question: Explain the `Element` or `Flatten` pattern.
interview.answer: `type Element<T> = T extends Array<infer Item> ? Item : T` matches arrays and binds their element type to `Item`. For non-arrays, the false branch returns `T`.
interview.followUp: How can the same pattern extract tuple elements? Match a tuple such as `T extends [infer First, ...unknown[]]` and use `First` in the true branch.

interview.question: What limitation applies when inferring from overloaded functions?
interview.answer: When a type has multiple call signatures, inference uses the last signature, which is generally the broadest catch-all signature. Conditional inference therefore does not choose an overload based on a supplied argument list.
interview.followUp: What happens with multiple inference sites for one variable? Covariant candidates produce a union, while contravariant candidates produce an intersection.

keyPoints: A conditional type can infer information from the type pattern it successfully matches, and expose that information in its true branch.
The standard extraction shape tests whether a type is an array, returns its inferred element type when true, and otherwise returns the input type.
`infer` introduces a named type variable without manually describing how to retrieve the matching part.
An inferred variable is scoped for use in the conditional type's true branch.
A conditional pattern may infer the same variable in more than one location.
gotchas: For overloaded function types, inference uses the last call signature rather than selecting an overload from argument types.
An `infer`-based conditional type cannot perform overload resolution using a list of argument types.
Do not place `infer` in an ordinary type-parameter constraint; it is valid only in the conditional type's `extends` clause.

Type manipulation::satisfies and as cons.summary: Combine `as const` with `satisfies` to validate a configuration against a required shape while retaining precise readonly literal types for later use.
Type manipulation::satisfies and as cons.explanation: Use `as const` to keep literal values precise and readonly, then apply `satisfies` to validate compatibility without replacing the expression’s inferred type.
Type manipulation::satisfies and as cons.syntax: const value = expression as const satisfies Type;

example.title: Validate while preserving literals
example.explanation: The assertion preserves literal and readonly information, while satisfies checks that every palette entry conforms to the required shape.

useCases.title: Typed configuration
useCases.scenario: Configuration objects need required keys and value-shape checking without losing literal inference.

useCases.title: Key-set validation
useCases.scenario: A fixed set of string keys must be checked for omissions or unexpected properties.

useCases.title: Precise APIs
useCases.scenario: Literal strings, numbers, tuples, and readonly properties should remain available to downstream code.

keyPoints: `satisfies` checks that an expression is compatible with a target type.
Unlike a type annotation, `satisfies` preserves the expression’s inferred type.
Use `satisfies` to detect incompatible values and missing or extra keys in configuration objects.

Type manipulation::Utility types.summary: TypeScript utility types are global helpers for transforming existing types. Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType, and Awaited reshape properties, map keys, extract function results, and recursively unwrap promises.
Type manipulation::Utility types.explanation: Utility types are globally available generic helpers that transform existing types. Partial makes every property optional, Pick and Omit select or remove properties, Record assigns one type to a key set, ReturnType obtains a function's return type, and Awaited recursively unwraps promise-like types.
Type manipulation::Utility types.syntax:
Partial<Type>
Pick<Type, Keys>
Omit<Type, Keys>
Record<Keys, Type>
ReturnType<Type>
Awaited<Type>

parameters.name: Type
parameters.description: The source type whose properties are transformed or inspected.

parameters.name: Keys
parameters.type: string literal or union of string literals
parameters.description: The property-key union selected or removed by Pick and Omit.

parameters.name: Keys
parameters.description: The key set used by Record.

parameters.name: Type
parameters.description: The value type assigned to each Record key.

Type manipulation::Utility types.returns: A derived type determined by the selected utility: transformed properties, a key-value mapping, an extracted function return type, or an unwrapped promise result.

example.title: Composing utility types
example.explanation: This example applies several global utility types to reshape existing types without rewriting their property declarations. Partial permits an update subset, Pick and Omit create narrower views, Record maps known keys to one value type, ReturnType extracts a function result, and Awaited recursively unwraps promise-like results.

useCases.title: Model sparse updates with Partial
useCases.scenario: HTTP PATCH or form updates

useCases.title: Create focused shapes with Pick and Omit
useCases.scenario: API response or view model design

useCases.title: Map a key union with Record
useCases.scenario: Exhaustive keyed configuration

useCases.title: Derive and resolve function results with ReturnType and Awaited
useCases.scenario: Async API typing

Type manipulation::Utility types.since: 2.1 for Partial, Pick, and Record; 2.8 for ReturnType; 3.5 f

interview.question: What are the differences among Partial, Pick, and Omit?
interview.answer: Partial<Type> produces a version of Type in which every property is optional, so it is useful for patch objects. Pick<Type, Keys> keeps only the named string-literal keys, while Omit<Type, Keys> removes them.
interview.followUp: How would you make a public DTO without an internal field? Use Omit<Internal, "internalField">; for an allow-list, use Pick instead.

interview.question: When would you use Record?
interview.answer: Record<Keys, Type> constructs a type whose properties are the specified Keys and whose values use Type. It is useful when every member of a known key union must have the same value shape.
interview.followUp: How can you require configuration for every route? Define a route-key union and use Record<Route, Config>.

interview.question: How do ReturnType and Awaited work together?
interview.answer: ReturnType<Type> extracts a function type's return type. Awaited<Type> recursively unwraps promise results, so Awaited<ReturnType<typeof load>> gives the resolved value type of an asynchronous loader.
interview.followUp: What happens with an overloaded loader? ReturnType uses the last overload's return type, so order and the final signature matter.

keyPoints: The listed helpers require no import because TypeScript exposes them globally.
Partial<Type> represents any subset of a type by making all its properties optional.
Pick<Type, Keys> creates a type containing only the selected keys from the source type.
Required<Type> is the converse transformation to Partial, making properties required.
Record maps a key set to a common value type, producing an object-shaped type.
ReturnType<Type> extracts what a function returns, including a promise type if that is the declared result.
Awaited recursively removes nested Promise layers and distributes across unions.
gotchas: ReturnType does not combine the results of overloads; it uses the last overload signature.
Awaited models await-like unwrapping rather than merely removing one Promise layer.

Type system::Function overloads.summary: Function overloads expose several checked call signatures for one function, followed by a single compatible implementation. The implementation signature is hidden from callers.
Type system::Function overloads.explanation: Define multiple public call signatures above one implementation. Callers are checked against the overloads, while the implementation signature must be compatible with them and is not directly visible to callers.

parameters.name: timestampOrMonth, day, year
parameters.description: A single timestamp, or a month/day/year combination, according to the overload selected.

Type system::Function overloads.returns: Date for each documented call form.

example.title: Overloaded date factory
example.explanation: The overload signatures expose the two supported call forms, while the implementation handles both internally.

useCases.title: Multiple call shapes
useCases.scenario: A function accepts different argument counts or arrangements that need distinct public call forms.

useCases.title: Input-dependent return types
useCases.scenario: Different input forms should provide different, statically known result types.

useCases.title: Typed API surface
useCases.scenario: A public API needs strict caller-facing signatures while sharing one runtime body.

interview.question: What is the difference between overload signatures and the implementation signature?
interview.answer: Overload signatures describe the call forms that callers may use. The implementation follows them and must have a compatible signature, but its own signature is hidden from outside code.
interview.followUp: What happens if a caller uses the implementation-only shape? It is rejected unless that shape is also represented by an overload signature.

interview.question: How does TypeScript decide which calls are allowed?
interview.answer: TypeScript checks calls against the overload signatures, not against the implementation signature. Each supported argument arrangement therefore needs a corresponding overload declaration.
interview.followUp: Why can an implementation with optional parameters still reject a two-argument call? Optional implementation parameters do not create public overload signatures.

interview.question: When should a union type be preferred over overloads?
interview.answer: Prefer a union parameter when one function shape can describe the alternatives without needing separate call relationships. Overloads are useful when different argument lists or argument-to-return relationships need to be exposed.
interview.followUp: What must remain true when overloads are used? Every overload must be compatible with the single implementation.

keyPoints: Overloads model several permitted ways to call one function.
The declarations before the body are the public overload signatures.
One implementation contains the runtime logic for all declared call forms.
The implementation signature supports checking the body but is hidden from callers.
The implementation must be broad enough to safely implement every overload.
gotchas: The implementation signature cannot be called directly; only the declared overload signatures are available to callers.
Use a union-typed parameter instead when the alternatives do not require distinct call shapes or return behavior.
A single overload signature followed by an implementation is not the intended overload pattern.

Type system::Generics.summary: Generics let reusable functions, classes, and interfaces work with many types while preserving relationships between inputs and outputs. Type arguments may be supplied explicitly or inferred from usage.
Type system::Generics.explanation: Generics introduce type parameters that stand for types supplied by callers. A function can use the same parameter in its input and output positions, preserving their relationship; callers may provide the type argument explicitly or let TypeScript infer it, while constraints restrict which types are valid.

parameters.name: Type
parameters.description: A type parameter representing the type captured from the caller; it can be supplied explicitly or inferred.

Type system::Generics.returns: The same captured type as the input, preserving the relationship between the argument and result.

example.title: A generic function preserves the input element type
example.explanation: The compiler infers T separately at each call, so the returned value preserves the element type.

useCases.title: Type-preserving functions
useCases.scenario: A utility should return exactly the element type supplied by its caller.

useCases.title: Typed collections and classes
useCases.scenario: A reusable data structure should retain the type of the values it stores.

useCases.title: Reusable libraries
useCases.scenario: An API should accept caller-defined types without sacrificing compile-time checking.

interview.question: Why use a generic instead of any?
interview.answer: A generic function declares a type parameter and uses it to connect positions in its signature, such as an argument and return type. This preserves the caller’s specific type instead of replacing it with any.
interview.followUp: How can callers choose the type? They can pass an explicit type argument in angle brackets or rely on type argument inference from the supplied value.

interview.question: How are generic type arguments supplied?
interview.answer: TypeScript can infer a type argument from a function argument, so callers often omit the angle-bracket type argument. Explicit type arguments are also supported when the intended type needs to be stated directly.
interview.followUp: What happens inside the implementation? The body must remain valid for every possible instantiation of the type parameter.

interview.question: What is a generic constraint?
interview.answer: A constraint limits the types that may substitute for a type parameter by requiring them to satisfy another type. This lets the implementation safely use members guaranteed by that constraint.
interview.followUp: Can constraints depend on other parameters? Yes; a type parameter may be constrained by another type parameter.

keyPoints: Generics let one component operate across many types while retaining type information for each use.
A type parameter is a variable at the type level, not a runtime value.
The parameter captures the caller’s type so later positions can refer to the same type.
A caller may explicitly provide a type argument when invoking a generic function.
Type argument inference commonly selects the parameter from the argument’s type.
Generic function types place their type-parameter list before the ordinary parameter list.
Classes and interfaces can both declare and carry type parameters.
gotchas: A generic parameter is not an unrestricted value type: the implementation must use it in ways valid for every type it could represent.
Do not assume operations or members that the type parameter’s constraint does not guarantee.
Constraints can relate parameters, but the relationship must still be expressed in the declaration.

Type system::Literal and primitive types.summary: Literal types model exact strings, numbers, and booleans instead of broad primitive values. Combine them in unions and object types to describe finite values and valid object states.
Type system::Literal and primitive types.explanation: TypeScript distinguishes broad primitive types such as string and number from literal types such as "published" and 200. Literal unions model a finite set of permitted values, while object types describe required properties and their types; inference can preserve or widen literals depending on whether a value is held in a const or mutable location.
Type system::Literal and primitive types.syntax:
type Name = "exact-string" | 42 | true;
type Shape = { property: Type; };

example.title: Exact values in an object shape
example.explanation: Literal unions restrict values to the exact strings or numbers declared, while the object type requires a matching set of properties and property types.
